opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because of the ConvNeXt work. In that project we took a standard ResNet and modernized it one step at a time toward a Transformer-like design, and what we kept finding was that a lot of the gap people attributed to "attention" or "Transformers being fundamentally better" was really explained by training recipes and a handful of design choices. So I've become fairly skeptical of architecture claims by default.

The first thing I'd want is a controlled comparison. The baseline should get the same training recipe, the same number of epochs, the same augmentation and regularization, and roughly the same compute budget. Many papers compare a new architecture trained with a 2021 recipe against a baseline trained with a 2015 recipe, and then the "architectural" gain is mostly a training gain. Just giving ResNet a modern recipe closed a surprising amount of the gap for us.

Second, I want the gain to hold up when you vary things. Does it survive across model sizes? If something only helps at small scale and the curves converge as you scale up, that tells you something very different than if the gap holds or widens. I'd also want it across several random seeds, because on some benchmarks the seed-to-seed variance is about as big as the claimed improvement.

Third, it should transfer beyond one benchmark. ImageNet top-1 is useful, but if the change is really better, I'd expect it to show up in downstream tasks like detection and segmentation, robustness evaluations, or a different data regime. A trick that only works on the exact benchmark it was tuned on is often just overfitting the benchmark.

Fourth, ablations that isolate the change. If a paper introduces five modifications at once, I want to know which one is doing the work. Often it's one or two, and the rest are along for the ride. Going step by step and reporting each step, even the ones that don't help, is one of the most honest things you can do.

And finally, I want to look at the cost side honestly: FLOPs, parameters, but also actual throughput and memory on real hardware. Some things look great on paper and are slow in practice.

So, briefly: same recipe, same budget, multiple scales and seeds, multiple tasks, clean ablations. If an improvement survives all of that, I'll believe it. Surprisingly few do, and I think that's an important lesson for the field. Simple, well-tuned baselines are much stronger than we tend to give them credit for.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing across model sizes, but does not specify unlimited compute or state-of-the-art model scale.

r002.rationale: It asks for a controlled comparison with the same training recipe and budget, not each architecture's own best hyperparameter settings.

r003.rationale: It calls for gains to transfer beyond one benchmark, including downstream tasks, robustness evaluations, and a different data regime.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because I've been on both sides of it. I've proposed architectures, and I've also spent a good amount of time trying to figure out whether other people's proposed architectures actually do anything.

The first thing I want is a fair baseline. That sounds obvious, but it's where most claims fall apart. When we did ConvNeXt, the whole point was that ResNets had been compared against transformers that got years of training recipe improvements, while the ResNet baseline was basically frozen in 2015. Once you give the old architecture the same recipe, the same augmentation, the same schedule, a lot of the supposed architectural gap disappears. So before I believe a new block or a new attention variant helps, I want to see the baseline tuned with the same care as the new thing. If the baseline numbers are just copied from an old paper, I discount the result heavily.

Second, I want to see the benefit survive a change in scale. A lot of tricks give you a point or two at small model size or small data, and then vanish, or even reverse, when you scale up. The reverse also happens, where something looks useless at small scale but matters later, but that's rarer. So I'd like at least two or three model sizes, ideally with a compute-matched comparison, not just parameter-matched. Parameter count is a poor proxy. If your module adds FLOPs or memory traffic, the right question is what you get at equal wall-clock or equal training compute.

Third, I want it to transfer. ImageNet accuracy by itself is a weak signal now. If the architecture change is real, it should show up on detection, on segmentation, on some out-of-distribution evaluation, or on a downstream fine-tuning setup. When an improvement only exists on the exact benchmark it was tuned for, that's usually a sign of overfitting the design to the benchmark rather than a genuine inductive bias.

Fourth, and this is underrated, I want to see the variance. Many architecture papers report a single run. On ImageNet the seed-to-seed noise is often a few tenths of a percent, and the claimed improvement is also a few tenths of a percent. So I'd like multiple seeds, or at least some honest statement about how noisy the setup is.

And finally, I care a lot about ablations that remove the new component and show the drop. If the paper has ten changes bundled together and the gain comes from the data pipeline, I don't want to attribute it to the architecture. Ideally each ingredient is added one at a time so you can see where the gain actually comes from.

I'll admit I also have a softer criterion, which is whether the idea makes sense mechanistically, whether there's a reason it should help. But I try not to lean on that too much, because the history of this field is full of things that made beautiful sense and didn't work, and things that seemed arbitrary and did. The empirical bar has to come first.

r001.rationale: The response asks for results at multiple model sizes, but does not require testing at state-of-the-art model scale or discuss unlimited compute.

r002.rationale: It calls for tuning the baseline with the same care as the new architecture, but does not clearly state that each architecture should use its own best hyperparameter settings.

r003.rationale: It says the benefit should transfer beyond ImageNet and appear on detection, segmentation, out-of-distribution evaluations, or downstream fine-tuning.

astra-6.text:
I would want to see a comparison where the architecture is really the thing that changes. If you also change the training recipe, the amount of data, or the compute budget, it becomes difficult to know where the improvement comes from. And the baseline needs to be strong and well tuned. Sometimes an older architecture looks much better once you train it with a modern recipe.

Then I would ask what we mean by a benefit. Is it better accuracy at the same training cost? Lower inference latency? Less memory? A model can look more efficient in terms of FLOPs and still be slower on actual hardware, so I would measure the resource that matters for the application.

Finally, I’d want the result to hold across multiple runs and, ideally, different scales or tasks. An ablation can help isolate which part of the change matters. A small improvement on one benchmark is interesting, but I’d be much more convinced if the advantage survives strong baselines and reasonable changes in the experimental setup.

r001.rationale: The response mentions testing across different scales, but does not state that the benefit should be demonstrated at state-of-the-art model scale if compute were unlimited.

r002.rationale: It calls for a strong, well-tuned baseline, but does not say each competing architecture should use its own best hyperparameter settings.

r003.rationale: It mentions different tasks, but does not call for demonstrating the benefit across diverse datasets.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to see a comparison where the architecture is really the thing that changed. If the new model gets a better training recipe, more compute, or more hyperparameter tuning, then it’s hard to know where the improvement comes from. And the baseline needs to be strong—you should give the existing architecture a fair chance with that recipe too.

Then I’d ask what kind of benefit we’re claiming. Is it better accuracy at the same compute budget? Faster inference on actual hardware? Lower memory use? Those are different claims, and parameter count or FLOPs alone won’t establish all of them.

I’d also want the gain to survive repeated runs and show up across a reasonable range of scales or settings. An ablation can help isolate which change matters. It doesn’t have to win everywhere, but we should understand where it helps and whether the improvement is large enough to justify the added complexity.

r001.rationale: The response asks for gains across a reasonable range of scales, but does not say to demonstrate the benefit at state-of-the-art model scale when compute is unlimited.

r002.rationale: It says the baseline should get a fair chance with the new model’s recipe, but does not call for comparing each architecture using its own best hyperparameter settings.

r003.rationale: The response mentions repeated runs and a range of scales or settings, but does not call for testing across diverse datasets.
